title: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
content: Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has claimed in an interview with the BBC. Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer. He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces. He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses. Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added. Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified. UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026. He says this difference in death toll – as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts – accounts for the current stalemate at the front. In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised." The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took. Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year. But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives. Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43. Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies. Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed. Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia. But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses. Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk. Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops. Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army. In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued. One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity". "In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained. The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said. He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come". He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said. Such technologies can give a new life to conventional weapons like tanks. Both Russia and Ukraine were now racing to develop "active systems of defence" to protect armoured vehicles, Syrskyi said. But he insisted that "the human role will remain definitive [on the battlefield] because [people] will need to control those systems". A 14-year-old was detained after the middle-school principal and teacher were injured. The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians face another winter with electricity outages. Ukraine's leader says he will support such a truce if Moscow does, after initially expressing surprise at Donald Trump's announcement. The US president made the announcement in a social media post, which was an apparent surprise to Ukraine and Russia is yet to comment. title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
content: US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34. "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC. He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided. Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series. "Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative, Sean Reilly, said in a statement to the BBC. Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's. He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said. The Brownsville Police Department confirmed the actor's passing in a statement to the BBC, saying the cause and manner of death have not been determined and the investigation remains ongoing. No foul play was suspected, according to police. The actor was declared dead on 12 October at what was believed to be his home, Cameron County Justice of the Peace, Cyndi Hinojosa, told the Associated Press, adding that a post-mortem examination would be performed. Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008-13. The anti-hero drama created by Vince Gilligan earned a whopping 58 Primetime Emmy nominations and won 16, including two for Outstanding Drama Series in 2013 and 2014. Cranston plays a high school chemistry teacher in New Mexico who turns to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. As he descends deeper into the underbelly of the meth trade, he drifts further from his son, Walt Jr, who makes his displeasure known with levity through much of the series. The actor posted a tribute to his on-screen son on Instagram, writing that he was in "deep despair" following news of Mitte's death. "I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm," said Cranston. "That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor." Cranston wrote of Mitte's advocacy for performers with disabilities, and noted that he never allowed his cerebral palsy to "be an excuse for anything". "All that promise and potential now is such a loss," wrote the actor, adding that he "thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed". "I'll miss you, son," he said. In a statement shared with the Hollywood Reporter, Aaron Paul, who played one of the show's lead characters, Jesse Pinkman, said he was at a loss and heartbroken. "RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed," he said. "And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that." Dean Norris, who played Mitte's uncle, Hank Schrader, posted that although "RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set". "He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed," Norris wrote. Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister's acting career in 2005. He had said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial. "Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn't end well for anyone," he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month. His character was based on Gilligan's late friend who had a more severe case of cerebral palsy and used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require. Mitte was seen as playing the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was never mentioned in the series. After shooting to fame, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible. "Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind," he told the BBC in 2021 . "Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change," he said. Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year. title: One dead and several hurt after rollercoaster incident at Six Flags
content: One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, an amusement park in the US state of Georgia. The Cobb County Police Department said it was investigating the fatality at the park, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta, according to the BBC's news partner CBS. Police did not specify what ride was involved, but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers. Six Flags Over Georgia said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones." Officials have not said how the person was killed. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials. Witnesses told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride, accounts that the BBC has not verified. Local outlet 11Alive quoted a witness saying the man fell from the rollercoaster on to the roof of a haunted house attraction. A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately, and they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident. Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation. The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five. Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico. The incident comes just weeks after one of its parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride. Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do". Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Thousands march to Indian Supreme Court to demand election chief resign
content: Thousands of opposition supporters marched through Delhi to India's Supreme Court to demand the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud. Monday's "March for Democracy" was the latest in a series of demonstrations, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital. Thousands of protesters were detained over the weekend. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi submitted a petition to the court challenging the process, in which tens of millions of names have been struck off the voter rolls. Opposition parties allege the revision benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the BJP reject the charge. For weeks requests to protest had been denied by police, citing law and order reasons. Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained in Delhi. Gandhi called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march. In a press conference, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to Chief Justice Surya Kant, laying out their concerns with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's alleged conduct. After they filed their petition later in the day, Kant responded by saying the matter was already before the court and therefore sub judice - meaning he could not speak about it. But he added: "You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with the law." There was a heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march, with restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some metro stations. A bus carrying Gandhi and other opposition leaders made its way to the court from Barakamba road. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind him was Neha Bora, a student leader who has gained prominence in the protests. A few kilometres on, in a place called Mandi House, the bus stopped and Rahul Gandhi and a few others climbed on top of the vehicle to wave at supporters lining up the street in the thousands. Many protesters climbed on to other buses parked here, while some waved flags and chanted anti-government slogans to the sound of drums and lots of cheering. "If they take away our right to vote, what is left with us?" one protester asked an AFP news agency reporter. Another protester called the march "a fight to save the very fabric" of India, the world's largest democracy. Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi. On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down. The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened. But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters. The Home Ministry has now announced demonstrations will no longer be permitted at Jantar Mantar. Three other sites have been listed as alternatives should permission be granted. The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the weekend protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders have said they will seek a new protest date from the police. Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. The BBC also captured footage of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters. In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists. "Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said. Rahul Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up. BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were. "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months," a local tells the BBC. A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and civilian resistance. Former students launched their own investigation, spending years collecting evidence and testimonies from others who say they were abused by the headteacher. Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and dozens of metro stations are shut to stop protesters from gathering. title: Watch: US man eyes pumpkin world record after fifth contest win
content: A five-time US giant pumpkin contest winner tells the BBC he'd "love" to break the world record for a second time. Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin from Minnesota to Half Moon Bay, California, for the annual pumpkin weighing event. His whopping gourd took home the prize, tipping the scales at 2,389 pounds (1,083kg). But Gienger says he's eyeing off a different prize – the world record title – which was set in England's south coast last week with a squash weighing in at 2,857 pounds (1,300kg). As a previous holder of the world-record mantle, Gienger says he's focused on the challenge ahead. WATCH: The BBC's Nadine Yousif meets the separatists who want to quit the country - and the Canadians calling for unity in the face of threats from US President Trump. The US death row inmate's legal team said at a press conference that she is now "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution. The BBC's Sarah Smith details the injuries sustained by the US death row inmate after two failed lethal injections, and what comes next. Canada's Parti Québécois has promised it will hold the province's third vote on independence, but said they won’t do so until Donald Trump is out of office. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. The BBC's Nada Tawfik was at the hearing, where the university's Student Assembly led a discussion around safety concerns and sexual violence on campus. The BBC’s Ione Wells reports from outside the Tennessee hospital where Pike is said to have arrived Wednesday night after surviving two lethal injection attempts. The family of Renee Good has announced two civil lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration. The BBC's Stephanie Hegarty looks at why two attempts to execute the US convicted murderer by lethal injection failed. The Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from Cape Canaveral with two Americans, a Russian and a Canadian who will spend up to six months aboard the International Space Station. Witnesses describe hearing Pike complain about pain in her arm, followed by sounds of breathing and snoring for almost an hour before she was taken to hospital. Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening. The BBC asked students in Washington about the allegations from a woman who says she was raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The 50-year-old Tennessee woman was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. The brown bear, described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months. Tau Robotics humanoids are remotely controlled by humans, and cost $30 per hour for house cleaning. The BBC's Ione Wells describes what happened in court, as the US mother's defence for the first time argued there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children. A former Cornell student is suing the university and seven fraternity members, claiming she was drugged and gang-raped in 2024. The mission was supposed to last 10 hours, but SpaceX announced it was ending after 90 minutes. A thunderous lift off, rapid satellite deployments and a fiery ending. title: Death threats and isolation - the cost of fighting sexual violence in Iraq
content: This story contains details of sexual violence which some readers may find upsetting "Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him . The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys. "Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him." One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says. Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim. "I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent." She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog. There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code. "Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred." Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to. Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation. Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing". Amal - not her real name - has been battling in court for about five years. She accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter - who was under 18 at the time - at gunpoint. She recalls her daughter's harrowing account of the incident, when she says the father walked into the girl's room and laid his weapon on her bed. She says he told her: "No-one will hear you if I kill you." Sexual abuse has long been seen as a taboo subject in Iraq. I have been in touch with many survivors who say that they prefer to hush it up, because of a potential family backlash. Others told us they were afraid to go to the police, for fear of social stigma and possible harassment. But Amal was determined to seek justice and rushed to police to report the incident. "She had lots of bruises around her wrists, as he held her hands tight. Whenever she tried to scream, he would cover her mouth with his hands," Amal says. Amal showed me medical documents, including DNA evidence, which support her account. A further demonstration of her ex-husband's cruelty came, Amal says, when she heard him tell a family member to "wash off our disgrace" if he was arrested. The expression is used in Iraq to refer to so-called honour killings - carried out in the belief that a woman has compromised a family's reputation. Amal says she believes the father threatened to put an end to his daughter's life "so the medical report would not be released and the assault would not be proven". She says her ex-husband is on the run and the court case remains open. "I fought all alone," says Amal, bursting into tears as she says her ex-husband hired several lawyers but she could not afford legal representation, and her family turned a blind eye to the situation. She no longer has any faith that a court ruling will come in her favour. "I just want him to stay out of my way forever," she says, with a sigh of despair. Amal's daughter is more fortunate than some women who have experienced domestic sexual abuse in Iraq, as she has a safe place to live. Many survivors have no independent income and nowhere to go. Iraq has very few shelters for abused women. Those we know of were established by an organisation co-founded by Yanar Mohammed, an internationally recognised women's rights advocate. Last March she was murdered outside her house in Baghdad by armed men. The perpetrators are still unknown. Experts working for the UN Human Rights Council wrote in April that Mohammed had been receiving death threats and online abuse for years, which were "believed to come from extremist religious militia". Activists repeatedly told us that targeted attacks on their colleagues have been on the rise in recent years. Hanaa Edwar, another prominent women's rights activist, says she saw Mohammed just two days before she was killed. She says she has also been threatened. "There are no laws, no protection, and no justice for women in Iraq," she tells me. "The problem in Iraq is not that women stay silent. It is that when they speak, very little in the system is built to listen, Mustafa Saadoon, head of the Iraqi Observatory for Human Rights, tells the BBC. "A woman who reports sexual violence has to get past her family first, then a police station, then a court, and at every one of those doors someone is likely to tell her to settle it quietly." Among the Iraqi women who say they feel failed by the system is Samira - not her real name. She tells the BBC that walking in the street puts her on the edge, after repeated harassments. Once, she says a man "was watching a porn movie on his phone and put it in my face" on public transport. In another incident in Baghdad, she says a man once followed her in his car for over 10 minutes. "It was extremely upsetting... I saw a police car. I went over and told them what had happened. They said they didn't have the authority to do anything." Although her mother is loving and supportive, Samira does not share any stories of sexual harassment with her. "If I tell my family, they will immediately ask me not to leave home in order to stay safe," she says. She has lost faith in state institutions: "Many men, including police officers, find nothing wrong with sexual harassment. If you are not a harasser, you are not a man, this is how they see it," she adds. Many women I spoke to in Iraq even accused police of sexual harassment. I put the accusation to Muqdad Miri, a spokesman for Iraq's interior ministry. "Cases of harassment involving police personnel happen but they are very few. They get a very harsh punishment, up to 10 years in prison and are dismissed," says Miri. I put it to him that some women were now documenting harassment on social media because they were afraid to report it to police. He said they were posting on social media because it was easier than filing an official report, and because doing so has become a common way to draw attention to a cause. I also put to him Samira's experience, in which she says an officer told her that he had no authority to stop harassment. Miri said Samira could have filed a complaint against this officer. There are no reliable statistics for sexual violence or harassment in Iraq. Miri told me that police have received about 300 reports of sexual violence since the beginning of the year. However, he accepts that the real number of cases is higher: "Many cases never reach the police because of society, customs and traditions." The stories of the women the BBC spoke to draw a picture of their battle not just against sexual violence itself, but against deeply entrenched mentalities and social beliefs that allow it to persist. Edwar has been advocating for women's causes for over 50 years and her assessment is gloomy: "Twenty-three years after Saddam Hussein's regime was brought down, it seems we are going backwards regarding women's rights." But both she and Jassim say they refuse to give up: "If all of us are going to get scared, no-one will change anything," says Sarah. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line. title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
content: Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out. Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress. Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome. Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent. One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s. It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%. Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate. But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years. The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them. Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November. But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner. The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party. Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House. Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three. The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them. Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years. Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way. Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate. But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats. They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent. And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally. Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters. The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US. The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation. Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration. Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years. Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system. Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected. One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage. At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (£303m). On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $400m held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement. The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising. More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact . Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups. Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party. Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against. title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
content: The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt. Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night. This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers. Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after. Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working. Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership. But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be. So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement? South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far. At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable." SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands. But how much of this was due to nationalisation? The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems. But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents. Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages. TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations. A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do. So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August. It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over. Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff. But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England. "The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers." Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats. But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working? "I think it's completely hopeless to try and do that assessment over such a short period," Stephen Glaister, a former chair of regulator the Office of Rail and Road who is now emeritus professor of transport and infrastructure at Imperial College London. He thinks a decade is needed to assess the impact of nationalisation. The government argues that official data suggests publicly owned train operators are performing better on punctuality and cancellations overall than those still under DfT contracts to private operators. Experts point out that whoever is running the passenger trains, some limitations remain. Many delays happen because infrastructure, like signals, fails. There's only so much capacity on the existing network. And getting better trains or more staff can take years. The view that privatisation ultimately failed, leaving unreliable services and high fares, may be widespread. However, Prof Glaister argues that for a few years in the 1990s, the old privatised system actually worked well. Operating costs and subsidies were falling while the number of train services and passengers went up, he says. And in the current context, it's important to be clear about what nationalisation really means. The railways Labour inherited weren't, in truth, completely privatised, and nationalisation doesn't mean a return to British Rail. For example, the infrastructure manager Network Rail has been fully under public control for over two decades. A number of train companies including LNER and Northern had already been nationalised under the Conservatives. Scotrail, Transport for Wales and Caledonian Sleeper are controlled by devolved national governments. And even those operators still on contracts issued by the DfT at Westminster have been heavily controlled by the government for years. During Covid, private operators started being paid a fixed fee to run services, while the taxpayer took on the financial risk. The terms of the contracts meant train companies had to "ask government for permission to blow their nose", according to one senior industry executive, who asked not to be named so they could speak freely. Highly profitable rolling stock companies ("ROSCOS") still own the actual trains. Freight companies operate privately too, and there are a handful of fully commercial "open access operators" on the rails like Lumo, Hull Trains and Grand Central - although there are concerns within the industry that these could end up squeezed. So what is often referred to as the nationalisation of the railways, in fact amounts to gradually returning passenger train operators run by private companies to public hands as their contracts expire - and making this the default. This is not all that's happening, though. The government hopes that re-organising the railways under a new publicly run body, Great British Railways (GBR), will make a big difference. This will bring together the running of trains and tracks, ending the current fragmented system. A botched rail timetable introduction in 2018 was the spark for the then-Conservative government to eventually propose GBR as a new overarching body - although the Tories believe private competition should not be excluded from the system. Some trains are already covered in distinctive GBR branding, but the organisation still doesn't exist. A new law to create it is making its way through parliament. Unknowns remain, like exactly how GBR will interact with devolved governments, and who its senior leaders will be. Transport expert and author Prof Jon Shaw, of the University of Plymouth, says the idea of a "single guiding mind" should create "a better planned railway that's more aligned to the customer". Prof Shaw thinks potential benefits include better long-term planning around rolling-stock and timetables, and the removal of "the compensation merry-go-round", where train companies and Network Rail argue about whose fault a delay was. Hynes says: "The way you get the railway to work is you get the infrastructure and the trains and the people working in harmony because it's a system. And we can do that in a publicly owned GBR railway in a way that we haven't been able to do for a generation." But Prof Shaw cautions of potential pitfalls. For example, "there remains very little money", and "a massive issue is whether or not the rail minister or DfT more generally - or the Treasury - will be able to butt out" and leave rail leaders to run the railway. Prof Glaister also fears politically sensitive aspects such as fares and levels of service could lead to politicians trying to run the railways themselves, because of the amount of public money involved. "Actually, governments are not very good at running railways," he says. "So you want management who are somewhat independent and able to run it." Lord Hendy insists that despite the Transport Secretary having ultimate sign-off on GBR's strategy, the body will be genuinely arms-length from government. "The point of this is to get a cadre of people who are committed to the outcomes that the secretary of state and I want for it, who can go off and run it on their own," he says, adding: "They'll have a lot more chance in the future than they've had in the last 20 years." The railways are currently subsidised to the tune of around £12bn a year - not including spending on major projects like HS2. The Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander says that she wants to see subsidy levels fall. Meanwhile, Network Rail has acknowledged a squeezed budget means difficult choices, and shoring up the network against the effects of more extreme weather requires investment. Prof Glaister says: "When the public is hoping for a better level of service, more reliability, fewer breakdowns and lower fares, what they're really asking for is more money to be put into the railway. "I don't think it's likely the government is going to be able to find more money, probably [it will have] less, actually. And so I think there's a real problem with ministers raising expectations from this policy." But Hynes doesn't see a contradiction between reducing taxpayer subsidy and making train services better. "My two north stars are performance up and subsidy down," he says. "If the service is better, we get more customers, we get more revenue." Lord Hendy and Hynes also push back on the idea that the answer to improving reliability might be running fewer trains. Hynes says: "In an industry with high fixed costs, the best way of getting the subsidy down is to go for growth." Questions also remain about how GBR will manage industrial relations. Terms and conditions currently vary across operators. What will cost-conscious ministers do if unions seek to standardise these at the most generous level across the network? While ministers argue they are getting on with improvements that people will notice, there's acknowledgement that the speed of improvement will vary between operators. Lord Hendy says some changes "ought to be dead boring… to make sure tomorrow is a little better than today if you can do it". But he says "more than 30 years worth of behaviors" will need altering to make the railway run solely in the interests of the customer. At Woking, is there optimism that things will improve in the long run? "I really hope so," says Leo, "it would be amazing - as it's not the best service now." title: On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
content: It was a journey at high speed through the desert - in a pick-up truck with armed fighters in the back. We were travelling with Yemen's pro-government forces, catching glimpses of the Arabian Sea, and forbidding mountain peaks in the distance. Houthi rebels were dislodged from here just days ago, we were told. When you are battling over expanses of empty desert, progress can be hard to see. But these soldiers, in Shaab-al-Jinn in Lahj governorate, showed us new sandbagged defences - new lines in the sand. "There was heavy fighting," said Tawfiq Al Haboun, a bearded commander in camouflage uniform. "They have snipers, artillery and ballistic missile launchers." Here in the far corners of the Middle East, a war is being waged with global implications. Yemen's entrenched civil war is now impossible to ignore. It's part of a wider conflict, stretching from Tehran to Riyadh, where missiles slammed into the international airport this weekend . Yemen's Houthi fighters – already a threat to global shipping – are an increasing threat to Saudi Arabia. And they provide leverage for their backers in Iran, Saudi's regional rival. Tawfiq Al Haboun pointed to shards of fibre glass and bits of metal at his feet – part of a downed Houthi drone that he said was carrying C4 explosives. Commander Al Haboun is from the Southern Forces, part of the loose – very loose – alliance of groups fighting for Yemen's government, which is internationally recognised, and backed by Saudi Arabia and its air strikes. The Houthis swept into the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, ousting the government. A year later a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened, trying to dislodge the Houthis. Despite years of devastating air strikes, that hasn't worked. The commander tells us about 500 Houthi fighters remain on high ground overlooking a strategic maritime corridor – Bab al-Mandab – connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The narrow waterway, which is crucial for oil exports, was just out of sight on our trip. The Houthis seized the area after a lightning advance in September. The commander claims pro-government forces have wrested back about 85% (the Houthis have denied losing territory in other areas but not here, as far as our local sources know). Until they regain complete control, there will be pressure on global oil supplies and on prices. We heard later that there were heavy clashes the day of our visit. Five military vehicles apparently hit improvised explosive devices planted by the Houthis. It's unclear how many fighters were killed or injured. As jitters run through international energy markets, hunger menaces weary Yemenis forced to flee this latest spasm of violence. Around 200,000 have been driven from their homes since the start of this escalation at the beginning of September, according to the International Organization for Migration - all this in the Arab world's poorest country. As we left the area, we saw a tableau of suffering with families dotted around seeking shelter under scrawny trees. Among one group of women and children we met Aisha, gaunt and elderly and sitting on the ground. She fled in fear from her home in the Kahboob mountains – an area which has been hit by Houthi drone strikes. "We have been here for 30 days," she told me. "I have no animals, no money, no water, no food, not even a blanket... we had to run, with just the clothes on our backs." At the weekend it was Saudi civilians at the international airport in Riyadh who were doing the running. The Houthi attack - the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade - sent shockwaves around the region and punctured the kingdom's sense of security. But in operating rooms in Yemen's port city of Aden, geopolitics feels remote. Hospitals are overstretched and doctors are working night and day to treat wounded government fighters coming from the front lines. We visited one military hospital where 51 casualties arrived in a single day – many with gunshot wounds, and several needing amputations. In a crowded ward, a Houthi fighter lay alongside fighters from the other side. Doctors tell us they make no distinctions. "I don't care where he comes from, his background or his religion. He is a human being so I should treat him as a human being, "said Dr Bassam Hazar. Even if the war ends, some will never leave it behind. One man was sitting silently on his bed, a white bandage wrapped around the stump of his left arm, and staples running along his crown. Others have not lost their fighting spirit, like Ahmed Ali Mahmoud who is smiling and animated, despite multiple fractures. "I am not waiting to be fully recovered," he tells us. "I just want to be able to stand. I think it is a religious duty and a national duty [to go back to fight]. The Houthis have destroyed the country. With victory I won't even feel these fractures." In the next ward lies 12-year-old Ali, a brown-haired boy, who is just one year older than Yemen's civil war. Ali was injured by a drone as he walked down the street and is facing a complicated surgery. "There is shrapnel near his spine," says Dr Amr Reyadh Assaqaf, standing by his bedside. "The operation won't be easy, but God willing our staff will be able to handle it." He tells me Ali is quiet and gentle. "At first he was depressed," he says, "but we gave him toys to play with and his mood is gradually lifting." But will war follow him into adulthood? A truce in 2022 brought a few years of relative calm. But now the Houthis are a stronger enemy, as they have proven at the weekend. They already control most of Yemen's population. If there is a new attempt at mediation – and there is some speculation about this - they may drive a hard bargain. Back at the hospital, as he prepares for the next wave of casualties, Dr Bassam Hazar hopes for change but doesn't expect it soon. "Maybe war is good for news," he says, "but it's horrible [for people]. "Sons are losing their fathers, and mothers losing their sons. We need peace." Correction 12 October: We initially reported that Aisha had said she was scared of Saudi air strikes. This was down to a translation error. In fact it was Houthi drone strikes that had been hitting her area. As election day looms, the president turns his eyes overseas for help with a pressing domestic problem. Footage from inside the airport shows the moment the strike hit on Saturday. The Saudi capital has been hit by multiple attacks from the Iran-backed Yemeni group over the weekend. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Saturday's attack was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since May 2015. title: Crew searching for Amelia Earhart arrives at crab-infested island
content: A team of researchers have arrived at a remote island to inspect possible plane wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart, who vanished in 1937 while flying around the world. The group from the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University arrived at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean on Monday. The search team's work, expected to take five days, could be hampered by giant land-dwelling crabs, as well as the El Niño climate phenomenon which is now the strongest ever recorded . Coconut crabs, also known as Robber crabs, emerge at night to hunt for small mammals and seabirds, and will force the search crew to spend nights on their ship for their own safety. The disappearance of Earhart, an American aviation pioneer who was attempting to circumnavigate the globe with navigator Fred Noonan, has spawned decades of speculation. Researchers will work to locate what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020. Some believe it to be the wreckage of her plane, but others have expressed scepticism that it is an aircraft at all, with one theory suggesting it is a collapsed tree. This is the first authorised trip to Nikumaroro Island in seven years, and the first visit to the Taraia Peninsula in more than 15, according to Purdue. The ship, the Marin Mainiku, on Monday arrived at the western side of the island, part of the nation of Kiribati, after a five-day voyage crossing 830-nautical-miles through the South Pacific. "It is incredibly rewarding to be this close to completing our inspection of the Taraia Object and potentially solving, at long last, the outstanding mystery of the disappearance of Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan more than 89 years ago," expedition leader Rick Pettigrew said in a blog post on Monday. On Tuesday, the crew plans to navigate through a narrow gap "blasted" in the atoll's reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited - to prepare for landing. The first day on the island will focus on "transporting equipment, clearing vegetation, and establishing staging operations", according to the post. One group of researchers will cut a trail through the jungle. Work will then shift to searching for evidence, including magnetic metals, on the Taraia Peninsula on Wednesday. Lastly, the researchers will use dredging equipment to move sediment for a visual inspection of the mystery object, which is believed to be located only 10 feet from the shore in as little as five feet of water (depending on the tides). Weather and ocean conditions "will continue to be a factor", researchers say, and El Niño could limit daily access to shore. Michael Krivor, a marine archaeologist on the trip, said he is currently concerned about a weather pattern traveling from east to west that could interfere with "safe transit in and out of the blasted channels". Another concern is the crabs, the largest land-dwelling invertebrates on the planet. "The crew will sleep nightly aboard the Marin Mainiku for a number of reasons, one of which is the presence of coconut crabs, whose size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical," the blog post says. Several theories suggest Earhart survived a crash on the island before being overcome by giant meat-eating crabs that carried away her bones. The crabs, which occupy atolls and desert islands throughout the South Pacific, can lift up to 28kg (62lbs), and are one of the only species that can crack open a coconut, although they also hunt for live prey like rats and birds. With a leg span of up to one metre and a body weight of more than 4kg, they are also the world's largest land-dwelling crustacean and are able to climb trees. In 2018, the International Group of Historical Aircraft Recovery used pig carcasses to demonstrate how the crabs were able to drag bodies to their burrows and strip the bones of flesh in less than two weeks. Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea, on 2 July 1937. From there, she and Noonan planned to travel towards Hawaii, but the plane vanished without a trace as they tried to reach uninhabited Howland Island, near Nikumaroro, to refuel. While there have been numerous theories about the disappearance, the official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems and, as she and Noonan struggled to find the island, the plane ran out of fuel and crashed into the ocean. title: Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections
content: With elections that will decide control of Congress just weeks away and American voters already casting ballots in some battlegrounds, President Donald Trump has turned his eyes overseas – and to Russia, in particular - for help tackling one of his most pressing problems. World affairs seldom provide easy answers, however, and developments elsewhere have threatened to undermine his efforts to bring down fuel prices before they provide any political benefit. A whirlwind weekend started on Friday afternoon, as Trump announced a new deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide the US with hundreds of millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel in the coming months. High energy prices, particularly for midwestern agricultural states that rely on diesel to power farm machinery and carry their goods to market, have been a growing source of frustration for American voters. Polls suggest they view the Iran War as the leading cause for their woes, and overall support for Trump, and approval of his handling of the war and the US economy in particular, has dropped precipitously. Trump heralded his Russian deal in a Truth Social post as bringing "lower prices for Americans," while he ordered his Treasury Department to suspend US restrictions that prevented Russian diesel from being sold on global markets. Two days later, Trump was back on his social media website, touting a new energy ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine. The truth, however, was more complicated. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had no advanced notice of the agreement, although he said his nation would abide by it. Russia, for its part, was silent. And on Sunday night, it launched a new wave of attacks on Ukrainian power plants. "It's clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelensky noted wryly on Monday. He added: "This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond." Trump and Zelensky have had a tumultuous relationship throughout his second term. The American president alternates between blaming Russia and Ukraine for the continuing conflict he previously said would be easy to end once he returned to the White House. In recent days, Zelensky has been the primary target of Trump's ire, as Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil infrastructure have contributed to worldwide energy shortages. On Saturday, Trump told reporters at the White House that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. And both the Financial Times and CNN have reported that the US has threatened to cut off arms sales and intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Zelensky does not halt attacks on Russian refineries. Zelensky "better damn well stop," Trump said. "I think that the president has a decade long public record of lashing out of people who aren't doing what he wants, when and how he wants to do it," Terry Haines, founder of independent think-tank Pangaea Policy, told the BBC. It now appears Trump's celebration of the "energy truce" may have been a familiar move for this president, touting an agreement before it had been sealed and delivered. In the past, for instance, he has prematurely announced Middle East ceasefires and sweeping peace agreements. Whether it is impatience on the president's part with the slow pace of diplomacy or a savvy negotiating tactic to push a deal across the finish line, the result has been to set off a scramble as the world decides what it means – and how to react. Those reactions didn't take long to arrive. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has become a vocal critic of the president's on the international stage, offered "strong support" for the energy ceasefire, but condemned the diesel deal as undermining peace and stability in Europe and helping Russia to finance its "illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine". In the US, Trump's diesel announcement prompted similar concern, even among members of his own party. Four Republican senators joined with Democrats in a letter calling on the president to "immediately reverse course". "Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the senators wrote in a statement released on Sunday. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law." What could be worse for the president than the criticisms is that the announced ceasefire has had little effect on the price of diesel, which continues to sit below its record highs but still well above $6 a gallon. Meanwhile, as the latest twists in the Russia-Ukraine conflict unfolded, new violence in the Middle East threaten to further strain global energy markets, regardless of what happens with Russian oil. A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia , including strikes on airports and energy infrastructure that killed at least 13 over the weekend, have threatened to escalate a decade-long conflict that had been simmering throughout the US-Iran war. "This is the Houthis sending a message that it's not just military targets, it's not just energy infrastructure, they're going to strike at civilian airports that could kill a lot of people," Michael Ratney, former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told the BBC. The US-Iran war was a conflict that none of the Arab nations in the region wanted, he said, and the latest Houthi offensive was a foreseeable result. With the US and Iran currently in an extended stand-off, any new hostilities could lead to more regional conflict and send oil prices soaring once more. "I do think it gets uglier before it really deescalates," he said. In recent weeks, Trump has pointed to Ukraine, not the Middle East, as the primary source of the world's energy woes. He cites increased oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had been effectively shut by Iran's military threat. That may, however, be wishful thinking – an attempt to convince the American public to direct their energy-related anger toward a conflict that began under a different president's watch. There is only one president at a time, however. And when American voters casts their ballots they tend to hold those who are currently in power responsible. After a rough weekend that again proved there are no easy fixes to the global energy crisis, that may be the worst news of all for the US president. Those outside the UK can sign up here . An in-depth look at the key polling, races and issues ahead of an election that will define Trump’s final two years as president. It comes after the armed group hit Riyadh's international airport and another facility, killing 13 people, in a significant escalation. title: Watch: CCTV shows people take cover after missile hits Riyadh airport
content: Two strikes on the international airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh have left 14 dead and more than 300 injured. There have been a series of other attacks earlier in the week. CCTV footage from inside King Khalid International Airport shows people taking cover as one of the missiles hit the building on Saturday. The Houthis in Yemen say they were behind the strikes and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace. The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The BBC's Middle East Correspondent visits kibbutz Nir Oz - one of the worst hit places during the 7 October 2023 attacks. An aeroplane flying to Israel fell 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes before it was diverted. Witnesses say Raseel's tent was hit by an Israeli helicopter strike. Israel’s military says it has no record of the attack. The BBC’s Nada Tawfik explains what happened even before the Israeli prime minister took to the stage at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The Israeli delegation cheered in support during Netanyahu's speech. Nada Tawfik in New York explains what happened. BBC's Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports from an area close to Israel's proposed site in the occupied West Bank. Six people, including three pupils at the Palestinian school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of Israeli settler-related violence. Republican Senator Lindsay Graham's funeral is bringing the two world leaders to town, where they'll separately visit the White House to discuss their region's wars. Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques, as well as cars and agricultural land in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say. Mojtaba Khamenei hasn’t been seen in public since March - but AI-generated images of him continue to spread online. The BBC's chief international correspondent looks at how Iran's new leadership will respond to several issues affecting the country. The US has launched the strikes on Iran in response to attacks on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Huge crowds have lined the streets of Tehran for the funeral procession of Iran's late supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The BBC's chief international correspondent Lyse Doucet is in Tehran, where funeral events are taking place in honour of Iran's former leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Authorities expect up to 20 million people to attend ceremonies across Iran and Iraq over the coming days. Iranian authorities say they expect millions of people to take part in funeral commemorations for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Dozens of boats are still anchored in the Strait, while ordinary Iranians try to continue to their lives. The BBC’s Daniel Bush is traveling with Secretary of State Marco Rubio as he seeks to reassure Gulf allies over the Iran deal aimed at ending the war. BBC correspondent Jessica Parker explains some key points of the direct talks between the US vice-president and Iran.
