title: ‘Just start shooting’: Death threats over data centers are tearing American towns apart
content: The handwritten warning was left at an Amazon data center construction site in suburban Virginia: A dozen pipe bombs scattered throughout the building would explode in the next half hour. Officers rushed to the scene as workers dropped their tools and fled. Bomb-sniffing dogs prowled every corner of the site. That April 22 message in the city of Manassas, authorities soon confirmed, was an empty threat – the latest in a string this year that has rattled the state and communities across the nation. As thousands of new data centers have been built to fuel the booming artificial intelligence industry, escalating public resentment against both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself is roiling small towns and suburban communities from coast to coast, a CNN investigation has found. Police have been called into action to investigate dozens of threats to data centers, from bomb claims etched on bathroom walls to online incitements to “use bullets on city council members” to suggestions that protesters should “unalive” pro-development officials, according to a CNN review of more than 100 police reports filed since last year. Aside from rare cases like an Indianapolis council member whose home was sprayed with gunfire, those threats have rarely led to actual violence – but they’ve eaten up hundreds of hours of police time, alarmed workers and inflamed communities already on edge over the projects. That rising outrage has also inspired a growing police crackdown, including federal agencies tracking data center protests and local cops questioning vocal activists, and even filing criminal charges against critics that have later fallen apart in court. The police records as a whole paint a vivid picture of a national backlash against the rise of data centers and AI reaching a boiling point at a moment when the debate has become a key issue threading party lines ahead of the midterm elections. They also show growing concern among law enforcement agencies about extremist groups at opposite ends of the political spectrum hopping on the anti-data-center bandwagon. “Anti-technology extremist narratives appeal to a broad array of ideological movements – including anarchists, environmental extremists, and white supremacists – creating a common target between otherwise opposing movements,” Colorado state officials warned in an April bulletin for police agencies. A similar California memo warned in June of “a broad range of threat actors… mobilized by AI-related grievances.” Still, some people who have been charged with making threatening comments insist they’re not extremists and do not actually wish violence upon anyone. Rather, they say they were driven to take dramatic action by rising electricity bills, environmental worries or fears of AI. “I’m not really political,” Anthony Hinojosa, an Illinois man arrested in February over an alleged data center threat, told an investigator who interrogated him, according to police recordings. “I feel like we don’t have a vote.” But elected officials say the reports show how the battle over data centers and AI is entering dangerous territory, where they’re fearing for their lives just for doing their jobs. Minneapolis council member Michael Rainville was left pleading in an August letter to his constituents for a more peaceful dialogue over the issue. “Please stop the threats against me and my family,” he wrote. In early February, police in Troy, Illinois fielded multiple calls about ominous statements on a community Facebook page. At the time, the city had been debating whether to clear the way for a roughly 200-acre data center that backers said could create hundreds of jobs. Like similar proposals around America, the once-anodyne pitch had become hugely contentious. Views of data centers have soured significantly this year. Nearly nine in 10 Americans say they’re more concerned than excited about the rise of these facilities, a CNN poll conducted by SSRS found in September. Amid that debate, Troy officials confronted a tirade on Facebook: “My hypothesis is no one would want to be shot at so just start shooting the people involved and it’ll never be built,” Hinojosa, a 33-year-old lawn-care businessman, commented beneath a post about the proposed data center. When a user asked if he was really suggesting violence, Hinojosa responded, “for sure,” screenshots of his posts show. Later that day, officers knocked on his door. “You’re being placed under arrest for making terroristic threats,” an officer said. “I think people are taking things out of context,” Hinojosa told the authorities. He said he had been upset about the proposed data center’s potential strain on electricity and water supply, but he insisted he would not hurt anyone and his words had been misconstrued. “Over a misunderstanding you are literally going to ruin my life,” he said. “It just feels like the mayor of Troy and the city council, they’re just not really listening to the public.” Hinojosa, who described himself in police recordings as a moderate Republican, now faces felony charges for intimidation and harassment through electronic communication. He has pleaded not guilty. His lawyer declined comment, citing an upcoming trial. Hinojosa’s case is one of about 70 among the police reports CNN reviewed that include allegations of threats, intimidation or planned attacks – a collection showing a striking range of anger at AI infrastructure that at times has spilled into serious claims of potential violence. Dozens of additional police reports detail other security concerns, including scuffles at county meetings, calls for police patrols at local officials’ homes and confrontations with data center staff. Some even describe explicit calls for assassinations. “Time to use bullets on city council members. Nothing is going to change until some of them are dead,” stated a post in August after officials green-lit site plans for a major data development in Westlake, Texas. “I’ll just shoot you in the face,” read another message described in a Salt Lake County, Utah case. In the Utah case, the alleged sender was charged in June with stalking and making multiple threats of violence along with other charges. His target, someone apparently linked to the project but not identified in court records, told police the ordeal led him to temporarily relocate his family and spend about $14,000 on home security. The case is pending. In Bell County, Texas, authorities arrested a man who allegedly threatened officials in an online screed that referenced the murder of a UnitedHealthcare CEO by Luigi Mangione. “We can always unalive them. Luigis Unite!” the comment stated beneath a post about local data center construction. His case is also ongoing. Police did not charge anyone in many of the incidents that clearly crossed the line into violent rhetoric. In some cases, threat recipients declined to press charges, such as in Archbald, Pennsylvania, where police heard about a voicemail in which a man threatened to “grab” the skull of a staffer for a data center development company and “smash it.” The man later apologized for “being an a**hole,” according to a police report. Other cases appear to have no suspects. That includes more than a dozen bomb threats at data center construction sites in multiple states including Iowa, Maryland, Utah and Virginia. In April, thousands of workers evacuated one of those sites in Eagle Mountain, Utah after someone wrote inside a portable toilet that a bomb had been set in a nearby building. One month later, authorities were called to the same site for the same reason and again found nothing, according to incident reports. The messages are often simple. “Bomb a data center,” read graffiti found at a Maryland construction site in June. “The bomb is ticking you better find it,” read another found at a Virginia site. The sheriff’s office in Loudoun County, Virginia – dubbed the data center capital of the world – has received reports of at least nine such bomb threats in less than a year, records show. A representative for an electrician business even complained to deputies that the frequency of bomb scares angered his colleagues because they were losing wages with the regular closures. “While each of these is handled with great urgency, the sheriff’s office is fortunate to have methods that enable us to quickly determine if it is a hoax,” Thomas Julia, spokesperson for the Loudoun County Sheriff, told CNN, adding that the expected prominence of data centers in upcoming elections “will likely mean more calls for service.” The flood of angry and at times frightening blowback to data centers has left police and lawmakers on edge around the country, CNN’s investigation found. Authorities have issued sweeping warnings of the potential for attacks, monitored activists and at times even arrested citizens for seemingly innocuous comments against data centers and those who support them. A West Virginia agency that analyzes threats, for example, shared a report about “potential risks” associated with a website that maps data center projects across the country. An office within the Department of Homeland Security forwarded the report to other agencies, records show. In June, US Capitol Police alerted law enforcement in an email about protests by Humans First, a group chaired by Amy Kremer, a conservative activist who helped organize the rally that preceded the January 6 Capitol riot. Kremer condemned the violence of the riot and was not accused of any criminal wrongdoing. The Capitol Police email in June noted her new group had coordinated “several demonstrations… targeting AI Data Centers.” Asked about that email, Kremer said, “That is unbelievable,” noting that her group is peaceful. “It is our right as Americans to protest, and we don’t condone violence.” Kremer argued the real threats authorities should scrutinize are AI and the companies behind it. “We do not have to give Big Tech a blank check and let them cram their technology and their infrastructure down our throat,” she said. Separately, among the incident reports obtained by CNN are more than a dozen that describe situations with no specific calls for violence by suspects that still triggered investigations or arrests. Police in El Paso, Texas questioned at least three data center opponents, including a woman who wrote to the city council, “we need to clear you out lol.” She later told investigators she simply wanted the officials voted out of office. In another case, a special unit looked into a woman who called a city representative and left a voicemail saying, “I hope you rot in hell and die.” She told investigators she had been repeatedly denied the opportunity to speak to the official about a local data center. “She feels threatened because I said ‘I hope’ – that is ridiculous. I’m threatened by the data centers,” the woman told El Paso police officers, according to body camera video. “We have to take everything serious,” an officer said. Separately, authorities in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania charged a man with making “terroristic threats” after he reportedly said he wanted local officials who supported a data center dead. A judge dismissed the case. Harley DeLander, a 28-year-old from Dixon, Illinois – a quaint community best known as the hometown of former President Ronald Reagan – learned while scrolling social media in May that a nearby plot of land had been promoted as a potential data-center site. Fearing what such infrastructure could do to the region’s water and electricity costs, DeLander lashed out at the head of a county association that had touted the land for development. “If he cared about his kids, he wouldn’t be actively trying to ruin the world they are being raised in,” DeLander posted on Facebook, along with a call for a protest at the man’s house and a statement that he “needs to have someone put the fear of god in him and his family. Make him scared to close his eyes at night.” The man, a former state representative, alerted Dixon’s police chief to DeLander’s comments, according to a police report. Authorities then charged DeLander with multiple felonies, including intimidation and cyberstalking. DeLander told CNN he then lost his job and was forced to wear an ankle monitor. Shocked and confused by the case, he retained an attorney and crowdsourced funds for his defense. After legal negotiations, he pleaded guilty to one petty charge lower than a misdemeanor and agreed to complete a court-ordered program to get the more serious charges dismissed. “I don’t regret my position toward data centers,” DeLander told CNN in an interview, noting that he received an outpouring of support from other data center opponents after his arrest and used the notoriety to further publicize his concerns. Officials in his city and county have stated there are currently no data center proposals under consideration for development, though DeLander fears that could still change. “I was an idiot for saying those things online but sometimes you have to be an idiot for someone to hear you. Sometimes you’ve got to do something foolish to get the word out,” DeLander said. The state’s attorney on the case, Charles Boonstra, declined to discuss specifics since the matter technically remains pending. Boonstra said DeLander was not prosecuted “because of his data center opposition; it was because of his incitement to violence and threats of violence.” Many Republican and Democratic politicians have pivoted away from backing data centers ahead of the midterms, but others – namely President Trump – have doubled down on their development. Amid these political debates, some extremism researchers warn that the risk of violence may be growing. They point to multiple would-be attacks that have already been disrupted. Last year, police in Ashland City, Tennessee arrested a man who said he purchased materials to burn down an xAI facility in Memphis; he told police he had gotten “wrapped up in politics” and “jumped too far down the deep end,” according to an incident report. In June, authorities charged multiple people in connection to an alleged plot to attack a UFC event at the White House. The mother of one of them told law enforcement the group held grievances including “data centers taking up all the water in communities,” and some of them also discussed attacking data centers in California, according to court records. Future attackers may not belong to any groups or even have exposure to the type of extremist content typically associated with threats, said Yannick Veilleux-Lepage, an associate professor at the Royal Military College of Canada who has studied AI-grievances and political violence. “You don’t need to be reading Ted Kaczynski to be radicalized against AI. You can simply listen to Sam Altman and Elon Musk talk for a couple minutes and that’s probably enough to radicalize some people,” Veilleux-Lepage said. Rainville, the Minneapolis council member who asked constituents to stop threatening him, told CNN he had not even taken a public stance on a proposed data center when he received intimidating messages. Those notes suggested they knew where he lives and what kind of car he drives. He said much of the opposition has falsely lumped all data centers together and presumed any development will inevitably drive up electricity costs and strain water supply. “You’re comparing apples and oranges, but that shows you the emotion, not only here in Minneapolis but around the country,” Rainville said.

title: Trump holds raucous Ohio rally as he tries to shore up base voters for GOP
content: President Donald Trump on Monday kicked off a week of red-state campaigning with a raucous rally in Ohio, where Republicans are fighting to hold onto a Senate seat that could be key to the majority . He spent portions of his nearly 90-minute remarks railing against Somali and Haitian communities, delivering red meat political attacks and catering to his base. He at times conjured two out-of-state Democrats — Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar and Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed — as bigger threats than former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who’s giving GOP Sen. Jon Husted a run for his money in a state that Trump had turned into a reliably red bastion. After Ohio, Trump’s scheduled to hit Alaska and Montana — states he won by 13 and 20 points in 2024 — as his team banks on him juicing base turnout in conservative areas. But on Monday night — as Trump returned to the same arena where he held a packed 2017 ‘thank you’ tour — large sections of seating on the left and right of the press riser, which came with prime views of the president, were empty. Still, it was a much livelier affair than some recent rallies, with two significant interruptions. At one point, a brawl appeared to break out between a protester wearing a “Release The Epstein Files” t-shirt and a rally-goer in the stands. Another interruption came from a young woman holding a Mexican flag. A big part of Trump’s pitch was about immigration, returning to a theme he hit hard in 2024, when he repeated his false claim that Haitian migrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating their neighbors’ pets. “Just look at what’s happening in the once great state of Minnesota,” he said, teeing up his attacks on Omar — a frequent target of his ire. Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday at the Washington, DC-area home of the congresswoman, according to a Justice Department spokesperson and a source familiar with the matter. And while Trump insisted he was not involved in that search, he went on to call Omar — who’s a US citizen — a “disaster” and attack the country where she was born. “[Rep. Omar] comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, without — all they do is shoot each other — and she comes into our country, and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said. “She’s got a constitutional right? She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” As he launched into into a tirade against Somalis in the US, supporters in the audience began chanting “Deport!” “They think they’re in Somalia, where they don’t have pants to wear,” Trump said at one point, going on to repeat his insult about “low IQ people.” He made blue-state Minnesota the foil. “If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked, and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed, we’re going to stop it. Just like we did with Springfield, we’re going to stop it,” Trump said. When the president turned to Brown — who holds a 6-point lead over Husted in CNN polling released last week — he tried to link the former three-term incumbent to national Democrats in more generic terms. “Sherrod Brown is the candidate of the Marxists, the communists, the anti-American radicals, who want to tear down America’s heritage,” Trump said, arguing that he also wants the Midwest “turned into Mogadishu.” Brown, a progressive populist first elected to the Senate in 2006, held onto his seat in 2018, during Trump’s first term, but lost reelection while on the ballot with Trump in 2024. “So, what happens is every time I run, we do great,” Trump said, repeating his call for voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this year. The first days of early voting in Ohio showed signs Democrats are more enthusiastic to vote , with affiliated Democrats making up larger shares of pre-election voters than they did two years ago, even in the most Republican parts of the state, according to data from the secretary of state’s office last week. (But Republicans in recent years have much been much more likely to vote early in person or on Election Day.) Trump seemed to tacitly acknowledge Ohioans’ previous tendency to back Brown, arguing that a vote for the former senator could have much wider ramifications. “It’s one vote, but that one vote can steer Congress into a direction that you’re not going to be happy with. And it’s not Ohio values.”

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar responds after federal officers search her home
content: Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday at the Washington, DC-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar , the Minnesota Democrat who has been the persistent target of ire from President Donald Trump’s administration, according to a Justice Department spokesperson and a source familiar with the matter. The congresswoman is running for reelection and the search warrant was executed only weeks before the midterms. It is unusual for the Justice Department to take such an aggressive investigative step toward a candidate so close to an election. Voting is well underway in Minnesota, with more than 127,000 people having already voted, according to data from the secretary of state. The Department of Justice said in a statement Monday that investigators from Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of the Department of Homeland Security that handles criminal investigations, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice.” “This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” a DOJ spokesperson said. The statement did not indicate what the investigation entailed. Omar called the search “the latest escalation” in Trump’s “campaign of political intimidation.” “I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote on X . “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.” Later on Monday, Trump called Omar “a terrible person,” but insisted he was not involved in the search of her home. “I understand they’re looking at her very carefully – I’ve always found her to be a totally crooked person,” the president told reporters at the White House, adding the search on Monday “has nothing to do with me.” “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ, I have nothing to do with it,” he said. House Democratic leaders called the search “deeply disturbing” and said it “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.” “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Whip Katherine Clark and caucus Chair Pete Aguilar said in a statement, adding that it comes with “less than 30 days until the midterm election.” A spokesperson for the congresswoman said in a statement to CNN, “For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back … The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong.” While authorities have not said what prompted the search, administration officials have previously indicated that Omar was facing an investigation. White House border czar Tom Homan said on Fox News last month that “things are going on” in relation to Omar, before adding: “But I can’t give the specifics of what’s happening.” Speaking to Fox on Monday morning, Homan confirmed the search warrant was executed, but provided no other information. “The specifics of the investigation, I think I need to turn that over to Todd Blanche or Markwayne Mullin,” he said, referring to the attorney general and DHS secretary. “I don’t want to get ahead of them commenting on an ongoing investigation.” One of Omar’s neighbors told CNN they were awoken around 4:30 a.m. Monday to the sounds of banging on doors. Later that morning, CNN observed that the home was surrounded by Homeland Security Investigations officers and that investigators were removing boxes from the home. Before leaving the scene, officials used a camera to document the condition of the house. Omar was born in Somalia and grew up at the peak of that country’s civil war. She fled to the US as a teenager and later became a US citizen. She was first elected to Congress in 2018 and became part of “ The Squad ,” a group of congresswomen of color known for pushing for progressive causes. Since joining Congress, she has been the target of racist vitriol, including from Trump, who called Omar “garbage” last year and said Somalis should “go back to where they came from.” Omar’s home district in Minnesota was the target of an expansive immigration-enforcement campaign earlier this year that led to violent clashes between protesters and immigration authorities and the fatal shootings of two US citizens. Top administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Mullin, have accused Omar of marrying her brother to help bring him into the United States. They have provided no proof of this claim. Homan said on Fox News last month, referencing Omar, that if “someone committed immigration violation, someone committed marriage fraud, or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law.” Asked specifically whether that means there was an open investigation into Omar, Homan responded: “I’m confirming that ICE is — yeah, like I said months ago, that is something that’s been reported and needs to be looked at.” In prior years, the department has treaded cautiously for the 60-day period before an Election Day to not make searches or levy charges that would disadvantage a candidate. Department policy also bars prosecutors and investigative agents from selecting timing in an investigation so that it would influence an election. Top Justice Department leadership signed off on the search after thorough deliberations given the proximity to the election, and a federal judge ultimately approved it, a source familiar with the investigation told CNN on Monday. The Justice Department also has special policies requiring additional approvals when investigations involve a member of Congress, and the Constitution provides additional protections for members around papers and communications that relate to their legislative work. This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Democrats are feeling America’s pain. Whether they can fix it is another question
content: Democrats may win the midterm election simply by exposing an unpopular president’s mirage of an economic “golden age.” But that won’t bring the price of groceries and gasoline down. On the campaign trail, Democratic candidates have effectively voiced the pain of families in the grip of the affordability crisis. They’re less good at nailing down specifics on how they plan to make life cheaper. And with the House looking increasingly likely to go blue and with Republicans sweating on the Senate, the question of whether Democrats could take tangible, fast action to ease Americans’ financial burden deserves more scrutiny. There’s some truth to President Donald Trump’s complaint that Democrats just turned the buzzword of “affordability” against him — especially since the Biden presidency saw inflation spike to its highest levels since the 1980s before falling back. “It’s fake,” Trump said at the GOP midterm convention. “They are so fake, because it was them that caused the affordability, to use their word, crisis.” Those are the breaks for an incumbent president — particularly one who called out the high price of groceries when he was running in 2024 and then failed to bring them down. Trump has been his own worst enemy, drowning out his own affordability plays — such as limiting taxes on tips and taking action to lower the prices of some prescription drugs — by choosing to wage Iran and tariff wars that sent costs soaring. But if Democrats were to win a share of Washington power on November 3, they’d also assume the burden of action — though their ability to reshape the economy would be constrained, in part by a president willing to wield his veto. That means a new Democratic Congress would have a greater capacity to thwart the most aggressive wielder of presidential power in modern history than to enact its own solutions. This could be a trap. Recent elections in the US and elsewhere in the democratic world show that voters quickly lose patience with parties that are elected to forge change but fail to deliver it. A Democratic honeymoon could therefore quickly fade. As the midterms race into the final three weeks, Democrats contemplating the possibility of a restoration in Congress face three questions: In a midterm showdown dominated by Trump’s cacophony and controversy, there’s been less attention on detailed Democratic proposals for a potential House or Senate majority in the 120th Congress. It’s not that there are no plans — there are scores of them. Candidates, interest groups and think tanks are churning out ways to bring down the cost of housing, raise wages, restore benefits, overhaul healthcare, protect workers from AI, introduce universal child care, launch a house-building boom, and slash the cost of groceries and gasoline. Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate nominee in North Carolina, touts his “Make Stuff Cost Less” plan. Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, who will appear at a CNN & Jubilee Town Hall on Wednesday, has a “ New American Dream ” agenda. Sen. Ruben Gallego has unveiled an expansive plan that includes a New Deal-style public service jobs program. Sen. Chuck Schumer could dust off a deeply detailed policy blueprint he futilely rolled out in a GOP Senate in January if Democrats win back the majority. But ideas won’t count for much without an actionable roadmap in what will be a fractured Washington if voters decide to deliver a rebuke to Trump next month. The country already intuits that turning to the Democrats won’t alone end an affordability crisis years in the making. In a CNN/SSRS poll in September , Democrats had a 7-point lead as the party Americans saw as closest to their views on the economy. But only 35% thought the party would have a mainly positive effect on the cost of living and a meager 27% said the same regarding their personal financial situation. Democrats would need to move fast. There’s two things they think they could do. “If we don’t stop this war, if we don’t stop it now, we are going to continue to watch as the Iranian regime chokeholds the Strait of Hormuz, making our energy prices higher,” Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said at a debate this month. “And you are going to pay for it both at the gas tank and at the grocery store.” And Cooper told voters in July that “we need to roll back these chaotic tariffs, and Congress needs to take back its constitutional authority on that — because that’s ending up costing everyday people and small businesses.” In theory, a new Congress could end the war and overturn Trump’s tariffs. But it would be almost impossibly difficult. Democrats could try to block new supplemental spending for military operations in Iran and pass laws to restrict how broader military funds are spent. But it would be a high-risk move since Trump could accuse them of deserting American troops in a war zone and could use his veto to block legislation. The failure of a Democratic House to stop the Iraq war after the party’s 2006 midterm victory is a daunting omen. And a war powers showdown with Trump over the dubious legality of the war seems as likely to produce a constitutional morass as to end the conflict. Congress could overturn the remnants of Trump’s tariffs that survived the Supreme Court’s rescinding of duties built on emergency powers. But a veto-proof two-thirds majority against the president might be a stretch in the Senate even if Democrats had overall control. If Democrats can’t immediately change the nation’s course, their political messaging will be even more critical. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in June that the first bill if the party wins the majority, HR.1, would be on affordability. “It will be hyper-focused on driving down the high cost of living and of course fixing our broken health care system as a part of that,” he said. His challenge would be in unifying the Democratic caucus behind proposed legislation given the ideological chasms between democratic socialists, progressives and moderates that were highlighted during this year’s primaries. Jeffries must hope for a larger majority than the minuscule one that has plagued GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson. But even if Democrats gain a healthy majority in the House, a Senate victory is unlikely to deliver anything but a narrowly divided chamber. Republicans will almost certainly still enjoy the capacity to block legislation if Democrats can’t amass 60 votes. Democratic priorities could be packaged into the kind of filibuster-proof reconciliation bills often used by the GOP. But presidents retain the veto — a power used, for example, by President Barack Obama to send back a GOP reconciliation bill in January 2016 that aimed to overturn the Affordable Care Act. It’s a quaint thought, but the US system of divided federal power does envisage compromise. Maybe Democrats could find an accommodation with Trump on housing affordability, prescription drug prices, child tax credits or infrastructure — issues that have interested the president in the past. But a promised Democratic onslaught of investigation targeting the Trump White House would surely precipitate a political cold war, making cooperation elusive. The most ambitious Democratic priorities — such as restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies — might only emerge from a show of strength in budget negotiations or potential government shutdowns. Such clashes are gambles for both parties. Elections perpetually conjure hope, promises and expectation. Divided government, however, usually results in bitter inertia. So an inevitable sequel may already be looming: yet another election, in 2028, on the same issue of affordability, as voters wait and wait for answers.

title: Trump is playing to his base in red-state campaign swing. But he’s often been dismissive of those voters
content: It’s been more than 10 years since President Donald Trump quipped , “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose voters.” His base isn’t nearly so devoted to him these days. But he still returned to the theme this weekend during one of his many recent stops in deep-red territory where Republicans hope he’ll turn out the base for the November midterms. “When you stand up here, it’s just like the love ,” Trump said at a rally in Tennessee. “I could say the stupidest things, and you clap. ‘Oh, I love you so.’” Both comments were couched as jokes, but both also pointed to a perception that Trump is happy to feed: that his base is almost cultishly devoted to him — as if they are unthinking automatons. A number of former Trump associates and advisers have said these kinds of comments betray a certain contempt that Trump has for his voters . And over the years, he has assembled a lengthy volume of comments that could be understood to be similarly dismissive of the base voters who Republicans are pinning their midterm hopes on. Let’s recap. Before Trump’s “Fifth Avenue” comment, he tried out a different version. “One of the things that came out in the one poll — nobody’s ever leaving me,” he said in New Hampshire in 2016, according to NBC News . “I could be the worst person in the world, they’re not leaving.” Trump said that even if he did “some really inappropriate things, my people stay.” “I have the most loyal people — did you ever see that?” Trump said in Sioux Center, Iowa, adding: “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose voters.” He added: “It’s, like, incredible.” “Even the really dishonest press says Trump’s people are the most incredible,” he said in Sparks, Nevada , just before the state’s caucuses. “I mean I had already 68% would not leave under any circumstances,” he added. “I think that means murder. I think it means anything.” After winning the caucuses, Trump pointed to his superior polling numbers among voters with less formal education, which has been one of his most loyal demographics over the years. But he rather provocatively called them the “poorly educated” — repeatedly. “We won with young. We won with old. We won with highly educated. We won with poorly educated,” Trump said, adding: “ I love the poorly educated .” In making an appeal to Black voters, Trump offered a pretty dismal review of their conditions. “Look, what do you have to lose?” he said in Michigan . “You live in your poverty, your schools are no good, you have no jobs, 58% of your youth is unemployed. What the hell do you have to lose?” As CNN’s Kevin Liptak noted late in the 2020 campaign, Trump’s pitch to voters often included saying he wouldn’t have visited their locales if he didn’t have to. He often pointed to the freezing weather. “Before the plague [Covid] came in, I had it made. I wasn’t coming to Erie,” Trump said in Pennsylvania. “I mean, I have to be honest: There’s no way I was coming.” In another jokey comment, Trump told people assembled in stifling heat in Las Vegas that he needed them to live so they could deliver for him at the ballot box. “Do you feel the breeze? ’Cause I don’t want anybody going on me,” Trump said. “We need every voter. I don’t care about you; I just want your vote. I don’t care.” A joke, sure. The crowd laughed. But six rallygoers were hospitalized for heat-related illness. “Their new SCAM is what we will forever call the Jeffrey Epstein Hoax, and my PAST supporters have bought into this ‘bullshit,’ hook, line, and sinker,” Trump wrote on social media about the push to release more documents related to Jeffrey Epstein. “They haven’t learned their lesson, and probably never will, even after being conned by the Lunatic Left for 8 long years.” Trump called these people “weaklings” who “do the Democrats work.” (Left unsaid: The fact that many of those who had pushed this story before he returned to office were his own high-profile supporters. That included some who went on to serve in major roles, such as FBI Director Kash Patel.) “When you stand up here, it’s just like the love ,” Trump said in Tennessee. “I could say the stupidest things, and you clap. ‘Oh, I love you so.’ It’s true.” After some laughter, the president assured that isn’t what he actually does. “But we don’t say the stupidest things,” he said. “We say things of common sense.”

title: New White House press secretary has a history of conspiracy-laced social media posts
content: President Donald Trump’s incoming White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, repeatedly made baseless accusations of pedophilia against prominent Democrats and shared conspiracy-related content, including claims that echoed the debunked “Pizzagate” theory and that Hollywood elites were pedophilic cannibals, according to a CNN KFile review of her social media posts. The posts, many from 2022, reveal a history of inflammatory rhetoric and conspiracy-related content from a woman now poised to become one of the administration’s most visible spokespeople. Zacharia also has a record of since-deleted social media activity that shows her advocating for hardline policies and criticizing the administration she is now poised to represent. She pushed for more aggressive action on immigration, suggesting in a series of now-deleted posts from June 2025 that the administration should suspend habeas corpus for migrants because the circumstances justified invoking the Constitution’s exception for cases of rebellion or invasion. The fundamental legal protection allows people to challenge their detention in court. Zacharia also publicly criticized the direction of Trump’s second administration, warning Republicans of a potential midterm “bloodbath” in a now-deleted tweet. In another deleted tweet, she shared a post accusing the Justice Department of covering up for people implicated in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. She also promoted on Truth Social a repost that claimed that comedian Joan Rivers died mysteriously after saying that former President Barack Obama was gay and that former first lady Michelle Obama had a penis. In response to questions about her previous social media activity, Zacharia said in a statement to CNN, “I am grateful to serve President Trump as Press Secretary, and I will diligently and effectively amplify his successful agenda.” In another statement, Steven Cheung, White House communications director, told CNN, “Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team. She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.” Neither the White House nor Zacharia addressed the content of the posts. Some of Zacharia’s since-deleted posts on X were first reported by The Bulwark. Her posts on Truth Social, the social media platform founded by Trump where she worked as communications adviser, remain publicly available on her account. In posts on Truth Social in 2022, Zacharia repeatedly accused prominent political figures and Hollywood elites of pedophilia, at times invoking conspiracy theories about powerful people sexually abusing children. “ Pedo Podesta. #pedoPodesta ,” Zacharia wrote in a September 2022 post about John Podesta, a longtime Democratic political operative and former White House chief of staff who had been a central target of the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy theory. The false theory emerged during the 2016 presidential election after Russian-linked hackers released emails belonging to Podesta, then Hillary Clinton’s campaign chairman. Conspiracy theorists falsely claimed the emails contained coded references to child sex trafficking and that Clinton and other prominent Democrats were operating a child sex abuse ring out of the basement of Comet Ping Pong, a pizzeria in Washington, DC. The restaurant did not even have a basement, and the baseless claims had real-world consequences when in December 2016, a North Carolina man armed with a rifle entered the restaurant and fired shots while attempting to investigate the supposed trafficking ring. Days after her first post on Podesta, Zacharia tagged Fox News host Sean Hannity and Trump in another post, asking why Fox News didn’t do a “ feature ” on “what a pedophile Podesta is.” In another post, Zacharia wrote, “ The radical left Hollywood elitists are sick pedo cannibals. Change my mind ,” responding to a September 2022 Variety article about actor Timothée Chalamet receiving a standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival for his role in “Bones and All,” a film about two young cannibals in love. Just weeks after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Zacharia also posted seemingly in support of Vladimir Putin, reposting a post that the Russian president was fighting a secret network of powerful elites. “Putin is at war with the CABAL - and the Ukraine is in bed with them,” read the post from an account named Richard Tomas, which included an image featuring prominent political figures, including Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and billionaire George Soros. Zacharia also reposted a baseless claim from Ali Alexander, a far-right activist who helped organize the “Stop the Steal” movement that promoted false claims of widespread election fraud following Trump’s 2020 defeat. “ Democrats want to mask and rape your children. That’s their satanic platform ,” Alexander wrote in an April 2022 post that Zacharia shared. Zacharia also reposted a September 2022 post from a Truth Social account called “Oinker” that compared then-President Joe Biden and anti-fascist protesters to Nazis, using the hashtags “#Antifa,” “#PedoHitler” and “#WrongSideOfHistory.” Zacharia also reposted the baseless conspiracy theory about former first lady Michelle Obama and the death of Joan Rivers. “Remember that time Joan Rivers said Obama was gay and Michelle had a dick then suddenly died?” read the July 2022 post that Zacharia shared. In another since-deleted tweet, Zacharia expressed frustration with the direction of Trump’s second administration, warning that the GOP could face devastating losses in the 2026 midterm elections if they didn’t shift course. In a December 2025 post, Zacharia responded to far-right commentator Mike Cernovich, who had criticized figures in the administration for focusing on media appearances, podcasts and cryptocurrency schemes rather than delivering on their promises. “We had our chance to save our country,” Cernovich wrote, lamenting that prominent figures were instead pursuing “vanity fair interviews, podcasts, and meme coins.” “ 2026 Midterms will be a bloodbath if we don’t shift course now ,” Zacharia replied. Zacharia also amplified an accusation that the Trump administration’s Justice Department was covering up for people involved in Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse of minors. On July 8, 2025, Zacharia retweeted a post from right-wing commentator Rogan O’Handley, known online as DC Draino, that questioned whether the Justice Department could be trusted. “I wish I could get excited about this,” the post read, discussing Trump plans to investigate former FBI Director James Comey and other officials involved in the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. “But if the DOJ will cover up for Epstein pedos, how can we trust them to go after these guys?” The repost came just a day after the Justice Department and FBI released a memo concludin g that investigators had found no evidence of an Epstein “client list,” and no credible evidence that Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals. The memo had sparked backlash from prominent Trump supporters, many of whom accused then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and other administration officials of concealing information about Epstein after years of promises to release additional records. In June 2025, Zacharia also called for suspending the constitutional right to challenge one’s detention in court. “ Suspend habeas corpus ,” she wrote in one post, first reported by The Bulwark. In two replies to White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, she urged suspending it “for reasons of Invasion,” citing the Constitution’s clause allowing suspension “in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion.” Miller had said weeks earlier that the administration was “actively looking at” the option.

title: MAGA watches another conspiracy theory blow up in its face
content: Two weeks ago, GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri saw his conspiracy theory about former special counsel Jack Smith implode spectacularly at a congressional hearing for all to see. Rather than seemingly learning a lesson from that episode, the MAGA movement in recent days embraced another sketchy theory that quickly fell apart — that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico was missing from the campaign trail because of a mental health episode. There have been plenty of such episodes this year. And it’s hardly just random social media accounts. The Talarico example is especially astounding for its reach. The idea that Talarico’s lengthy absence from the campaign trail was not due to the flu (as his campaign said), but rather a mental health episode quickly spread far and wide. Over just a few days, it went from an admitted rumor ; to some like former Los Angeles GOP mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt claiming they had actual sources ; to winks and nods from Talarico’s GOP opponent Ken Paxton and President Donald Trump ; to right-wing sites covering the still - baseless claims ; to some attempted independent journalism that has been repeatedly promoted by Elon Musk . By Sunday afternoon, a pair of right-wing influencers shared audio of what they said was a call with a mental health center in Ohio seemingly confirming that Talarico had just been released from its facility. “Looks like he was just discharged this evening,” a voice is heard saying. “That’s why I don’t have it.” The story then exploded on the right. But it just as quickly fell apart: Some on the right are now deleting their posts about the false claim . Others like former Trump adviser Caroline Wren are walking back the significance of the claim. One of the two right-wing influencers who shared the audio, Nick Sortor, appeared at the White House last year during a roundtable on antifa. For what it’s worth, as CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski has noted , Talarico did a virtual event on September 30 where he said he had the flu and looked physically unwell. He was then off the campaign trail for nine days — not the two weeks that many on the right have claimed — before reemerging publicly on October 9. Talarico also has type 1 diabetes, which can make flu symptoms worse . But for the MAGA movement, this is merely the latest conspiratorial episode. Two weeks ago, it was Schmitt presenting what he seemed to view as smoking-gun evidence that Smith had been at an Atlanta Hawks game in February 2024 and — the theory seemed to go — might have been coordinating with local prosecutors who had indicted Trump in Fulton County, Georgia. Except it turned out Smith was actually at a basketball game in Maryland that night. And even if he was in Atlanta, it would have proven basically nothing . Back in July, MAGA figures led the charge in embracing rumors and even flat-out claiming that GOP Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky — an unpopular figure among Trump supporters since he declared the president lost the 2020 election — was brain dead, amid his much-longer absence from public view. GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin even cited a claim that a photo of McConnell was AI-generated , before later backing off. A GOP House member even said he didn’t know whether McConnell was alive . McConnell later returned to the Senate. Over the summer, many on the right embraced Trump’s baseless conspiracy theory that vandals had sabotaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. A conservative reporter posted supposed video proof . Trump’s Justice Department even indicted a former Olympian. But the Justice Department later acknowledged that the damage “ was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism .” In June, Republicans far and wide — including elected officials — suddenly promoted theories suggesting voter fraud was to blame for Pratt failing to make the runoff in the Los Angeles mayor’s race. Except the theory rested on a complete misreading of the data and was debunked even by Trump’s DOJ and a top local GOP official. Pratt’s showing was also very much in line with how Republicans usually perform there. And, strategically, it would have made no sense for incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass to rig the system to promote a fellow Democrat, who would have a better chance at beating her in the runoff than Pratt. And in February, many on the right shared supposedly damning evidence from right-wing influencer Nick Shirley citing 30 allegedly illegal voter registrations at a UPS Store in San Diego. Those promoting the story included Donald Trump Jr. , who accused the media of ignoring it. But fact-checkers noted that the UPS Store was actually on the ground floor of a mixed-use building with residential units above it. California elections officials said none of the registrations used the UPS Store’s suite number. Of course, it’s entirely possible that the people promoting these theories don’t necessarily believe them — and that they just see value in promoting them, regardless of how true they are. Some MAGA influencers, after all, continued to promote Schmitt’s theory even after it fell apart . It would seem especially expedient to promote such rumors about Talarico, given he has continued to lead Paxton in some Texas Senate polls and could give Democrats a crucial win in their quest for a Senate majority. Or, as one participant on an X Spaces event about the Talarico story put it on Sunday: “Whether it’s true or not, people deserve to know the potential of this.” Regardless of whether these people have a gullibility problem, the MAGA echo chamber now has a well-established credibility problem. This story has been updated with additional developments.

title: Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU
content: Andy Burnham has promised a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s future place in Europe, saying the existing relationship is “not good enough” as he framed next month’s Brussels summit as a possible first step to EU membership. The prime minister said Britain must take a “clear-eyed rational look” at its long-term relationship with the bloc to boost economic growth and control immigration, which needed to go beyond Labour’s existing red lines. The next “reset” summit will take place on 20 November, ending months of uncertainty, with the two sides seeking to sign deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading, which Burnham hopes could provide a £10bn-a-year boost to the economy. One EU diplomat said a deal on the three “significant but modest” issues needed to be approved as a test of the UK’s good faith so both sides could get on with the “real reset” in the longer-term relationship. But the UK remains braced for a possible row over protectionist “Made in Europe” trade rules amid industry fears they could lock out UK manufacturers, prompting the prime minister to pledge he would raise concerns with his EU counterparts. Burnham was also forced to clarify that he did not think Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit campaign had affected the final result, after he raised questions about the legitimacy of the outcome in comments at the weekend. In a statement to MPs, the first since the party conference recess, an otherwise confident-sounding Burnham said it would be a “major dereliction of duty” for his government to turn away from exploring closer relations with the EU. “We should not turn our backs on this opportunity and I hope all sides of this house will get behind the government’s efforts to land a positive outcome,” he said. “I believe our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have. “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country. “Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.” Burnham denied he was reopening the Brexit debate, insisting he respected the referendum result, but added that he wanted to take a “pragmatic approach” to boost economic growth and improve cooperation on migration. He was forced on to the back foot over his remarks on a podcast on Sunday that Russia had interfered over Brexit, rejecting suggestions from Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, that he may have been loose with his language. “It is a matter of record that Russian actors sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time,” he said. Burnham had said on Sunday it was clear that Russia had interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum after he sought answers when he arrived in No 10. He did not disclose who gave him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or, crucially, whether any interference had affected the result. Downing Street said the prime minister “absolutely” accepted the Brexit referendum result and believed it to be legitimate, while the foreign minister, Stephen Doughty, said it was clear Russia had attempted to interfere but had failed. In his statement, Burnham told MPs they were right to raise the question of the “loss of immigration control” that came with Brexit, as Labour grapples with continuing public concern over the issue, and suggested Brussels recognised this. The UK is excluded from Eurodac, a database that holds biometric and ID data to identify asylum seekers and irregular migrants, and exited the Dublin regulation, a legal mechanism to return refugees to the European country through which they had first entered or transited. But while the prime minister told MPs a return to free movement was “not on the table” in his discussions with the EU, and said he would honour Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines, he was unable to rule it out for a post-election future. Sources on both sides believe they will be able to get other issues over the line at the summit next month, suggesting that a food and phytosanitary agreement would have been reached in July if the summit had gone ahead on its original date. Issues still to be resolved include a transition period for grains grown in the UK using recently approved fungicides not yet licensed in the EU. This would allow farmers harvesting this year to sell stockpiles next year even with the different regulations. The thorniest issue remains the youth mobility programme, allowing EU and British citizens under 30 to live, work or study in each other’s countries for up to three years. The two sides are at odds over the overall numbers, as well as the tuition fees students would pay at British universities. The biggest current risk to the UK of not aligning more fully with the EU is being locked out of the new Made in Europe initiative – aimed primarily at imports from China in strategic sectors such as renewable energy, nuclear and electric cars – which will block British-made components being used in EU supply chains. EU sources have insisted there can be no agreement on the issue with the UK at the summit, because the bloc is yet to agree its own position on the proposals. EU lawmakers hope to agree a position on a key proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, in December. But Brussels is, at least, open to discussing the issue, and it may be part of the summit statement – a joint text agreed by both sides. The UK has the support of the Netherlands, Poland and Italy for inclusion in the scheme, but France in particular has posed a stumbling block. Burnham acknowledged that Made in Europe presented “risks” to British manufacturing, perhaps in an attempt to address some concerns inside government that Downing Street hasn’t been prioritising the issue. He said: “It is important that we get to an arrangement here that works for both the UK and the EU. After all, we’re both trying to deal with the same issue, which is Chinese exports and the damaging effect that is having on our industry.”

title: Revealed: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firm
content: A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian can reveal. Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in the operations of Redfield & Wilton Strategies and used it to develop potential campaign strategies, according to several sources who have worked there. The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate. As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear. Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under which quotes were published by the Washington Post newspaper. As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties. Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative. The rules of the British Polling Council do not require pollsters to state any political affiliations, but they have strict guidelines on how they must declare who has commissioned and paid for any polling. In a statement, Rodrigues, the company’s sole director, said there had never been “an institutional, polling, research, commissioning or financial relationship” between Redfield & Wilton and Reform UK or Farage. He said Bruni-Lowe had worked as a “consultant” from mid-2020 until late 2022, and returned “voluntarily” in the summer of 2025 to train interns. Rodrigues added that Bruni-Lowe was “an important and highly valued member” of the team. Sources said Bruni-Lowe, who some employees said had been known as “Chris Redfield”, was heavily involved in the company’s polling operations. Rodrigues said the surname Redfield was used as an email account convention within the organisation, citing other examples of “Philip Redfield” and “Bruno Redfield”. He said: “It was not a device created specifically for Chris and it did not conceal his identity from people working within the company.” Nonetheless, the situation was confusing enough that at least one newspaper, the Washington Post, attributed quotes to that name, while notes taken by one former employee during an oral induction in the summer of 2021, and seen by the Guardian, described “boss – Chris Redfield is COO essentially”. Rodrigues said: “He was never presented to staff as the company’s chief operating officer and staff were never instructed to treat him as such.” He added that Van Scheltinga, as director of research, led the “day-to-day operation”. The Guardian can also reveal that Dan Jukes, then a senior adviser to Farage, sought to promote Redfield & Wilton’s work in 2020, looking to place exclusive polls in publications including the Guardian, which turned down the offer. Jukes stepped down as Farage’s chief of staff recently over a scandal in which undercover reporters posed as potential overseas donors to Reform UK. Footage published by Channel 4 News showed the co-founder of polling firm JL Partners, James Johnson, apparently acknowledging that Jukes had commissioned polling funded by an overseas donor. The polling had appeared in newspapers without any reference to the party, with JL Partners acknowledging “weaknesses” in its procedures. Jukes denies wrongdoing and Reform UK has said the party itself did not commission the work. On Wednesday, Reform announced that an internal inquiry had cleared the officials of breaking the law . The matter remains under police investigation. Redfield & Wilton started producing polls in 2020 with little information about the people behind the company. During its publicly active years before it became less visible in late 2024, its voter intention polls frequently appeared in politically influential newsletters from Politico, the Times, and the New Statesman. Bruni-Lowe ran Farage’s 2015 election campaign, helped test messaging for the formation of the Brexit party and advised on the 2019 local elections campaign, as well as having produced private polling for Farage since at least 2014, apart from during a brief period of working for Rishi Sunak before the 2024 election. In his book on political strategy, he writes of having worked for “organisations and candidates of all political persuasions”. He is considered to be part of Farage’s inner circle and was close enough to the Reform UK leader to have been present on a trip to party donor Christopher Harborne’s Thai wellness retreat at Christmas in 2022 to mark the crypto billionaire’s 60th birthday. Other guests photographed at the meeting include Farage’s unpaid aide and convicted fraudster George Cottrell. In May 2023, Van Scheltinga and Bruni-Lowe were photographed having drinks at a Mayfair restaurant with Farage, Cottrell and Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader. One source said he suggested the firm’s work could be sold to political parties, and that Bruni-Lowe appeared “obsessed” with the dossier. Research by employees included freedom of information requests to councils to find expenditure on translation services. Rodrigues said the FOI project was a “commercial research project” and translation services were just one of “several dozen categories” examined by the company in a project led by Van Scheltinga. He added that none of the research was supplied to Reform or Farage. The company’s other work, sources said, included polling in Montenegro, Hungary, Hong Kong and the Bahamas, as well as research about attitudes in the UK to gold and cryptocurrencies. Employees were not always told exactly how their work would be used. According to one former employee, they were told their work on a foreign election would be for the Telegraph, but the polling never appeared in the newspaper. Another said they believed their work on cryptocurrencies was for a client. One unusual piece of work by the company was an October 2021 submission to an inquiry into central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) carried out by the House of Lords economic affairs committee. The company cited polling it said “was self-funded internally by Redfield & Wilton Strategies Ltd for the purpose of this submission”. The submission said the scepticism of the British public over the UK government’s capacity for innovation meant “it is strategically important that alternatives to a CBDC from the private sector, including those that are already in use, are also given the opportunity to be developed further”. According to a person who worked at the company at the time of the submission, “all of the crypto stuff came down from Chris [Bruni-Lowe]”. One online profile for Rodrigues, a solicitor based in London, refers to him holding a directorship of an “innovative market research firm”. However, according to former employees, he had a limited role in the day-to-day running of Redfield & Wilton. One source said that at a rare in-person meeting Rodrigues was “paraded around on a laptop on a Zoom call”. Van Scheltinga was frequently quoted giving analysis of the company’s polling and wrote columns for the Times and Telegraph. Van Scheltinga was the listed contact for the company with the British Polling Council, the trade body for pollsters, but one industry source said he never attended BPC meetings. This led to demands from the BPC for a representative of the group to appear before them: that was ultimately Rodrigues, the nominal director, who maintained “total silence”, according to the industry source. Bruni-Lowe declined to comment. Van Scheltinga did not respond to requests for comment.

title: If Russia had interfered with the Brexit vote, Nige would have been the first to know
content: L et’s face it. The very idea that Russia may have tried to interfere with the Brexit referendum is clearly absurd. I mean, what could a hostile state hope to gain from sowing division between the UK and the EU? We all know that Vladimir Putin has nothing but the best interests of European democracies at heart. That’s why he invaded Ukraine. To help it become a bit more democratic. The sort of democracy which is so highly prized that 99% of its citizens vote for its leader. If only others could be more like Russia. If anything, Putin would have wanted the UK to remain within the EU and it was only his impartiality that prevented him from saying so. Besides which, why would the Russians want to get involved in anything so politically insignificant as the partial break-up of an organisation it considers an enemy. It just makes no sense. And it’s not as if Russia has any track record of clandestine foreign engagement. Next people will be suggesting Russia paid Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, at least £30,000 to make helpful speeches in the European parliament and recruit other MEPs. Andy Burnham sees it rather differently. Over the weekend he claimed that since he had become prime minister he had seen incontrovertible proof that the Russians had been involved in a misinformation campaign during the referendum. He didn’t say exactly what form the interference had taken. Merely that it was a reality. So it was no surprise that Nigel Farage was asked for his reaction during a Reform press conference in Kent on Monday morning. “The prime minister is a liar,” Nige snapped. “Yes, a liar.” Nige was beside himself with anger. He is getting more thin-skinned by the day. This was yet another myth fabricated by the Establishment. Another excuse to try to relitigate the result of the referendum. The whole thing was clearly a plot to undermine him. Everything that ever happens in the world somehow always becomes personal to Nige. His solipsism eclipses everything. We all only exist as satellites of his own imagination. When he dies, we will all die with him. If he hasn’t killed us first. It was like this. If Russia had tried to interfere with the referendum then he would have been the first to know about it. And frankly he had been deeply disappointed that no one had tried to buy him. Numerous punters had bought him for £80 a pop on Cameo. But despite having billions in petro-roubles, the Russians had blanked him. First the sound, then the fury. You can almost sense Nige’s desperation these days. It had all been going so well for so long. Reform had been 10 points clear in the polls for the best part of 18 months as Labour and the Tories flatlined. Nige was even being taken seriously as a possible next prime minister. Then along came the financial scandals and the election on the nod of Burnham and suddenly Farage found himself marginalised. His politics of grievance were no longer quite so attractive. Yet Nige can’t help himself. Logic would suggest that if the public mood was shifting more back to the centre ground of traditional two-party politics, then he would be better off heading in that direction himself. Instead, the Mr Nice Guy carapace – “I’m only saying what you’re all thinking” – is falling away. Nige is revealing himself to be a deeply unpleasant person all along. There is no longer the pretence of “let’s just have a pint and some bantz”. Everything has become actively nasty. Retreating to the safe ground of the 15% for whom nothing can ever be nasty enough. So much so that Nige is even back to sharing a platform with Zia Yusuf. A man who makes Honest Bob Jenrick look trustworthy. Almost cuddly. The Reform roadshow was in Kent to promote Nige and Zia’s war on immigrants. The UK had been invaded and everyone had to go. No exceptions for migrants with winning smiles or tragic backstories. There was no room for Afghan women and children. This was Toxicity Unfiltered. Prejudice 101. The Americans had removed their bombers from RAF Fairford because of the small boat crossings. He didn’t pause to wonder why the US president had kept some planes at other UK airbases. There would be tariffs on any countries who didn’t want their migrants back. Maybe even airstrikes. Asylum was just a scam, Zia insisted. He would starve the migrants in small boats. Refuse them medicines. Any civil servants who declined to activate the mass deportations would be lined up and shot in front of the white cliffs of Dover. Come the end we were treated to Nige’s stream of unconsciousness. Ukraine? Well, everyone had their limits and he was a bit fed up with Zelenskyy. You couldn’t go on supporting your allies indefinitely. And what had happened to the Sun? Not so long ago it would print any old bollox Nige told its reporters to write. Now they were daring to be nice to Kemi. It was an outrage. A stitch-up. Back in the Commons in the afternoon, you could almost feel the years peeling away in a return to the Brexit wars of a decade ago. And that’s without Burnham even suggesting the UK rejoins the EU. All he said was that he would try to reset the relationship in a way that worked for all parties and would grow the economy by £10bn a year. At all stages the British public would be boss. This was far too much for Kemi. Natch. She accused the prime minister of undermining the referendum result – for, er, speaking the truth – and that she would much rather the economy had zero growth than it came at the cost of closer ties with the EU. It was quite like old times. How I’ve missed them.
